name: Shwethalyaung Buddha
significance: A 55-metre reclining Buddha west of Bago, traditionally credited to King Migadippa in 994 CE and reckoned the largest Buddha image in pre-colonial Southeast Asia. Twice abandoned to the jungle, it was rediscovered by British railway workers in 1881 and sheltered under an iron pavilion in 1906.

name: Kyauktawgyi Buddha Temple
style: Modelled on the Ananda Temple at Bagan
significance: Royal temple at the foot of Mandalay Hill housing a Buddha carved from a single block of pale green Sagyin marble, consecrated in 1865. Begun by King Mindon Min in 1853, it took until 1878 to finish after a palace rebellion and other disorder stalled the work.

name: Nanpaya Temple
style: Brick, stone and mud-mortar shrine with a square sanctum, mandapa and perforated stone windows
significance: A rare Brahmanical shrine in the overwhelmingly Buddhist landscape of Bagan, said to have served the captive Thaton king Manuha before being turned into a temple. Its four stone pillars carry celebrated reliefs of Brahma seated on lotuses.
story: Its sculpture shows Vishnu reclining on the serpent Shesha with a lotus rising from his navel to give birth to Brahma, the creation of the cosmos.

name: Shri Kali Temple, Yangon
significance: Built by Tamil migrants in 1871 when Burma was governed as a province of British India, this temple anchors the Hindu community of downtown Yangon's Little India. Its roof is densely covered with painted images and stone carvings of Hindu deities.

name: Laykyun Sekkya
significance: A standing Buddha of 116 metres (129 metres with its base) raised near Monywa on the initiative of the abbot Ven. Nãradã and completed in 2008. It briefly ranked as the tallest statue in the world and stands beside a reclining Buddha depicting the Mahaparinirvana.

name: Buddha of Kyaikhtiyo
significance: A seated Buddha of 77.9 metres at Kyaikto, raised over a seventeen-storey pagoda whose height was fixed to echo the Buddhist year 2556. It was opened in April 2019 to coincide with the Buddha's Birthday festival and feeds pilgrims free of charge.

name: Kailashnath Mahadev Statue
significance: A 44-metre Shiva in steel, concrete, zinc and copper standing above the Araniko Highway at Sanga, funded by Kamal Jain and the Hilltake group. Built from 2003 and opened on 21 June 2011, it is described as the tallest Shiva statue in the world.

name: Bindhyabasini Temple
significance: The principal Shakta temple of Pokhara, established around the 1760s and given a royally appointed priest by King Girvan Yuddha Bikram Shah in 1815. Its hilltop compound also holds shrines to Saraswati, Shiva, Hanuman and Ganesha.
story: The goddess is held to be Yogamaya of the Vindhya hills in India, brought to Pokhara by royal order after a king's pilgrimage vision.

name: Ichangu Narayan Temple
significance: One of the four great Narayan shrines of the Kathmandu valley, ascribed to the Licchavi king Haridutta in the 5th century and rebuilt in the 18th. Its courtyard is set with images of Garuda and Mahalaxmi, and its idols have been stolen and recovered more than once.

name: Adinath Lokeshwar
significance: A hilltop shrine at Chobhar to one of the four Lokeshwars of the Kathmandu valley, revered by Buddhists and Hindus alike; built in the 15th century and rebuilt in 1640. Visitors know it for the pots, pans and other household vessels nailed across its walls as offerings.
story: The image is said to have been fished out of the river by Suval Acharya and installed on Kacchapala hill, where an annual bathing rite was founded for it.

name: Budhanilkantha Temple
style: Open-air shrine around a single black basalt image
significance: An open-air shrine north of Kathmandu whose five-metre black basalt Vishnu lies on a coiled serpent in a 13-metre recessed pool. The image is over 1,400 years old, is venerated by Buddhists as well as Hindus, and is protected under Nepal's ancient monuments act.
story: The stone is said to have been struck by a farmer's plough and unearthed by chance; King Pratap Malla's vision that a monarch who looked on it would die early has kept Nepal's kings away ever since.

name: Ambikeshwori Temple
significance: A Shakta temple on the bank of the Katuwa Khola a short way north of Ghorahi, counted among the Shaktipeethas and known locally as Maiko Than, the Mother's Place. Shivaratri, Teej, Dashain and Kalratri are its principal festivals.
story: The Swasthani Purana holds that this Shaktipeetha arose where the right ear of Sati fell to earth.

name: Arjundhara Dham
deity: Arjuna, with shrines to Shiva and Hanuman
significance: A pilgrimage complex 6 km north of Birtamode in Jhapa, built around a spring associated with the Mahabharata hero Arjuna. A gurukul for Brahmin students and a cow farm are maintained in its grounds.
story: During the Pandavas' exile Arjuna is said to have loosed an arrow into the ground here, and water burst from the spot.

name: Kasthamandap
significance: A great wooden public pavilion beside Kathmandu Durbar Square, later given an inner shrine to the yogi Gorakshanath; excavation with radiocarbon and OSL dating placed its oldest fabric in the Licchavi era of the 7th century. It collapsed in the 2015 earthquake and has since been rebuilt.

name: Pumdikot Shiva Statue
significance: A 51-foot Shiva on a white stupa base, 108 feet in all, set on a ridge above Pokhara at 1,500 m and ringed by 108 Shiva lingas. Completed in late 2021, it is the second tallest Shiva statue in Nepal.

name: Dantakali Temple
significance: A hill shrine above Bijayapur in Dharan, kept as a Shakta seat and thronged at Navaratri and Dashain. Its name joins danta, tooth, to the goddess Kali.
story: The temple is held to mark the place where the teeth of the goddess Sati came to rest.

name: Chandeshwori Temple
significance: A 17th-century pagoda temple on the Punyamata river a kilometre from Banepa, carrying carved struts and a vast painted Bhairava said to be the largest wall painting in the Nepal Mandala. Its outer wall bears a mural of the goddess killing the demon Chanda.
story: The goddess is said to have destroyed the demon Chanda, whom Shiva's boon had made invulnerable to all but a woman, after he felled the tree she hid in; a lingam grew from his body and stands in a small shrine nearby.

name: Andhimul Temple
significance: A pagoda temple at Satrasay Phant in Tanahu District built in 2035 BS, its Shivalinga installed in 2054 BS. It draws pilgrims from Tanahun, Kaski, Gorkha and Lamjung and closes through the month of Shrawan and on new-moon days.
story: The name is explained by a girl who came searching for water and found a spring here, from the local words aan, thirst, and dhi, water.
